title: Metta, revisited
hook: kindness wishes well; its near enemy is clinging affection (Visuddhimagga 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmavihara, and your line: four rooms to live in. Could you name all four from memory? Kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity. Day two hundred thirty-three, and the first room.

Some love feels like a gift, and some feels like a grip. You've probably been on the receiving end of both. The friend who's glad when good things happen to you, even when it means you move away. And the one whose affection comes with strings: text me back, need me, don't change. Both call it love. Both might even feel warm from the inside. But one leaves you free and the other doesn't. A Buddhist manual written fifteen hundred years ago drew exactly this line. Today: metta, revisited.
screen: `A GIFT, OR A GRIP.` → `LOVE WITH STRINGS.` → `ONE LEAVES YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: You met metta in camp three: kindness, loving-kindness, from mitta, a friend. The phrases, the benefactor, the difficult person, the six directions. Now we go deeper, with help from the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, a great manual of meditation written in Sri Lanka by the monk Buddhaghosa in the fifth century. Its ninth chapter describes each of the four rooms with a kind of map. Metta's mark, it says, is promoting the welfare of others. Its job is to prefer their welfare. It shows up as the melting away of ill will. Then comes the surprising part. Every one of the four rooms, the manual says, has two enemies. The far enemy is the obvious opposite, easy to spot. The near enemy is sneakier: it looks like the real thing, feels like it, and quietly takes its place. For metta, the near enemy is greed, clinging affection, the kind of attachment that wants something back. It's near, the manual explains, because both kindness and clinging notice what's good in a person. One says, may you be well. The other says, may you be mine. So metta succeeds, it says, when it makes ill will fade, and it fails when it turns into sticky, selfish affection. That's why the manual suggests starting metta not with a romantic partner, where the line blurs easily, but with yourself, and then a benefactor, someone who has helped you, like a teacher. None of this means affection is wrong. Families and friendships run on it. The point is to know the difference from the inside: kindness wishes well, and lets go.
screen: `METTA — FROM MITTA, A FRIEND.` · `THE MAP OF THE VISUDDHIMAGGA.` · `NEAR ENEMY: CLINGING AFFECTION.` · `MAY YOU BE WELL, NOT MAY YOU BE MINE.` · then, large: `KINDNESS, NOT CLINGING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you love. Offer them the old wish, silently: may you be well, may you be happy. Now look, gently, underneath the wish. Is there any string on it? A wanting them to stay, to need you, to turn out a certain way? If there is, don't scold yourself. Just see it. Then try the wish again, with the string cut: may you be well, however your life turns out. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Metta. Kindness that wishes others well; its near enemy is clinging affection, which looks warm but wants something back.
Your line: kindness, not clinging. Today, check one kindness you offer for strings, and see if you can give it with none attached. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions teach the near and far enemies from the Visuddhimagga, so students can tell real kindness from its look-alikes; metta practice often begins with oneself or a benefactor rather than a romantic partner.

match.prompt: match each piece of the manual's map of metta.

myth: the Visuddhimagga says affection is always wrong
it warns that metta fails when it turns into sticky, selfish affection; families and friendships run on affection.
the near enemy is dangerous because it looks like the real thing
both kindness and clinging notice what's good in a person.
the manual was written in Sri Lanka in the fifth century

fork.setup: a friend is moving across the country for a job they've wanted for years. you'll miss them. what does metta sound like here?
options: 'may you be well, and thrive there.'
say nothing and hope it falls through.
fork.reveal: the manual's line: kindness says 'may you be well'; its near enemy, clinging, says 'may you be mine'.

original.note: Pali mettā: kindness, loving-kindness, from mitta, a friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: metta just means feeling love.
what it means: kindness that wishes well and lets go; its near enemy is clinging affection.

what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX gives metta's characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause, names raga (greed) as the near enemy and says metta fails when it produces sineha, selfish affection.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (metta: characteristic, function, near and far enemies)

notes: Visuddhimagga IX is paraphrased throughout; no public-domain English translation on the approved list.
Near enemy of metta: raga (greed/lust), 'because both see virtues'; far enemy: ill will (vyapada). Failure: producing selfish affection (sineha). Confirm section numbers (approx. IX.93, IX.98).
Advice to avoid a romantic partner as an early metta object: Visuddhimagga IX (the 'dear one' and opposite-sex cautions); rendered gently.
Buddhaghosa dated to the fifth century CE, working in Anuradhapura.
Audit 2026-09-30: Visuddhimagga IX advises against starting metta with a very dear friend; the starting order now reads oneself, then a benefactor such as a teacher.
